# Draft:Eli Ward child sexual abuse survivor Church of England sally cahill

----
Eli Ward
Eli Ward is a British abuse survivor and safeguarding advocate. He came forward publicly in 2013 to report historical child sexual abuse by Robert Waddington, Dean of Manchester Cathedral from 1984 to 1993. His testimony was instrumental in the subsequent independent inquiry into the Church of England’s handling of abuse allegations. Early Abuse and Delayed Disclosure Ward joined the choir at Manchester Cathedral in 1980 at approximately age eight. Beginning around age 11, he was groomed by Waddington and subjected to sexual abuse that continued into his teenage years. The abuse included overnight visits to Waddington’s home, where Ward slept in Waddington’s bed from age 13 onward. Ward did not disclose the abuse at the time of its occurrence. In 2003, Ward reported the abuse to a counsellor in England. His sisters subsequently reported to Manchester Diocese that their brother had been abused, but were told no action would be taken until Ward himself made a formal complaint in person. 2012 Police Report and Public Disclosure In October 2012, following media coverage of the Jimmy Savile abuse case, Ward reported the abuse to Greater Manchester Police. He subsequently came forward publicly in May 2013 when The Times published an investigation into allegations against Waddington. Unlike other victims, Ward waived his right to anonymity, identifying himself by name in media coverage. Greater Manchester Police launched an investigation in October 2012, concluding that no criminal charges could be pursued because Waddington had died in 2007. The Cahill Inquiry (2013–2014) Ward provided evidence to the independent Cahill Inquiry, commissioned by Archbishop John Sentamu in July 2013 and chaired by Her Honour Judge Sally Cahill QC. The inquiry examined how the Church of England handled allegations of abuse by Waddington between 1999 and 2005. Judge Cahill’s report, published in October 2014, documented Ward’s account of grooming and abuse. The report noted that while Waddington’s former Archbishop, David Hope (later Lord Hope of Thornes), received allegations about Waddington in 1999 regarding abuse in Australia, he did not report the matter to police or take sufficient protective action. The report concluded that Hope’s “concern for the welfare of Robert Waddington seems to have been paramount in his response to these allegations.” Aftermath and Advocacy Following publication of the Cahill Report, Ward stated: “I want no other child, person, to go through what I have gone through. I have been through the full range of emotions — that’s terrible, disgraceful. I should have been enjoying life, getting on with it — my abuse has stopped me doing that.” The Cahill Inquiry made eight recommendations for improvements to Church child protection procedures, leading to policy changes including the establishment of a National Safeguarding Team and National Safeguarding Adviser role within the Church of England. Ward’s case was subsequently included in the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA) investigation into the Church of England, which published its findings in 2020 and criticised the institution’s systemic failures in child protection.
